title: Water on the Knee: Why Your Knee Swells and Whether the Fluid Should Be Drained
seoTitle: Water on the Knee: Should the Fluid Be Drained?
metaDescription: Why fluid collects in a swollen knee, when draining it helps, why it can come back, and which signs mean you should be seen the same day.
intro: 'Water on the knee' is extra fluid inside the knee joint. It is a sign, not a diagnosis: the knee is reacting to something, such as arthritis, an injury, gout or, rarely, an infection. Draining the fluid can ease tightness and help find the cause, but on its own it does not fix the reason the fluid built up.
summary: Water on the knee is extra joint fluid caused by arthritis, injury, gout or infection. Draining it can relieve tightness and the fluid can be tested, but it often returns unless the cause is treated. A hot, red, very painful knee, especially with fever, needs same-day care.

sections.heading: What is 'water on the knee'?
sections.body: It is an effusion: more fluid than normal inside the knee joint. A healthy knee holds only a small amount of lubricating fluid. When the joint lining is irritated, inflamed or bleeding, extra fluid collects, and the knee looks puffy, feels tight and is hard to bend fully. The fluid is the knee's response to a problem, not the problem itself. Swelling that sits outside the joint, such as over the kneecap after kneeling, or a lump behind the knee, can have different causes and is assessed differently.

sections.heading: What causes fluid in the knee?
sections.body: The cause is usually injury, arthritis, crystals such as gout, or infection. How quickly the swelling appeared and whether there was a twist or fall are the most useful clues. A review in American Family Physician notes that swelling within four to six hours of an injury suggests bleeding into the joint, often from a significant ligament, bone or cartilage injury.

table.caption: Common causes of a swollen knee and the usual story behind each. A guide only; an examination is needed to tell them apart.
rows: Gradual, comes and goes, often after a busy day or long standing
Treatment of the arthritis: exercise, weight, pain relief, sometimes an injection
Twist or fall, swelling within hours
Examination and often a scan; urgent if you cannot bear weight
Sudden, very painful, red, often without injury
Fluid testing to confirm, then medicines to settle the attack
Hot, red, very painful knee, often unable to move it; fever in some people
Emergency care: draining, fluid testing and antibiotics
Swelling in more than one joint, morning stiffness
Blood tests and a rheumatology opinion

sections.heading: Should the fluid be drained?
sections.body: Sometimes, but not routinely. Draining (aspiration) is done for two reasons: to find out what is causing the swelling, and to relieve a tight, painful knee. If the swelling appeared without an injury, testing the fluid is often the most useful step, because it separates infection, gout and inflammation from wear-related arthritis. For a mild, familiar flare of known arthritis that is settling, drainage is often unnecessary.
bullets: When it helps: a new swollen knee without injury, especially if hot or red; a large, tight effusion limiting movement; a bloody swelling after injury where relief makes the knee easier to examine
What happens: after cleaning the skin and numbing it, a needle is passed into the joint and fluid is drawn off. It is usually an outpatient procedure taking a few minutes
What the fluid shows: clear yellow fluid fits arthritis; blood suggests injury; cloudy fluid raises concern for infection or crystals, and is sent for testing
Risks: uncommon, but include bruising and, rarely, introducing infection, which is why it is done under clean conditions

sections.heading: Will the water come back after draining?
sections.body: It often does if the underlying cause is still active. Draining removes the fluid that is present but does not stop the joint lining producing more. This is why treating the cause matters more than the drainage. In arthritis, that means strengthening exercise, weight management and pain relief, sometimes with a steroid injection after drainage. Repeated drainage without a diagnosis is not a plan; a knee that keeps refilling deserves a proper assessment.

sections.heading: When is a swollen knee an emergency?
sections.body: A knee that is suddenly hot, red, very painful and hard to move or bear weight on should be seen the same day, even without a fever. These are the signs of a possible joint infection, which the NHS advises needs urgent medical help. Infection can damage the joint quickly, and diagnosis needs the fluid tested before antibiotics are started.
bullets: Hot, red, very painful swollen knee, with or without fever
You feel generally unwell, shivery or feverish with a swollen joint
Swelling after an injury and you cannot take weight on the leg
A swollen knee that has had surgery or a knee replacement, especially if new and painful
Diabetes, a weakened immune system, or steroid or biologic medicines, with a newly swollen knee

sections.heading: What can I do at home, and what will the doctor check?
sections.body: For a mild swelling without red-flag signs, short-term rest from aggravating activity, a cold pack, elevation and simple pain relief are reasonable for a few days, while keeping the knee gently moving. A doctor will ask how and when the swelling started, examine the knee and, depending on the story, arrange an X-ray, drain and test the fluid, or order blood tests. An MRI is mainly useful after an injury or when the cause remains unclear.
bullets: Avoid heating a knee that is already hot and red; get it checked instead
Do not let anyone drain the knee repeatedly without explaining the cause
See a doctor if swelling has not settled within about a week, keeps returning, or the knee locks or gives way

faqs.q: What causes water on the knee?
faqs.a: Extra fluid in the knee is a reaction to a problem in the joint. The common causes are osteoarthritis, injuries such as ACL or meniscus tears, gout or pseudogout, inflammatory arthritis and, rarely, infection.

faqs.q: Should water on the knee be removed?
faqs.a: Not routinely. Draining is useful when the cause is unclear, especially if the knee swelled without an injury, because the fluid can be tested. It also relieves a tight, painful knee. A mild flare of known arthritis that is settling often does not need it.

faqs.q: Does the fluid come back after it is drained?
faqs.a: It often does if the cause is still active, because draining removes the fluid but does not stop the joint producing more. Treating the underlying cause, such as arthritis or gout, matters more than the drainage.

faqs.q: Is water on the knee serious?
faqs.a: Usually it is not an emergency, but it should be explained. A hot, red, very painful knee that is hard to move, with or without fever, can be a joint infection and needs same-day medical care.
Most people find it uncomfortable rather than painful. The skin is numbed first, and many people feel relief once the pressure from the fluid is reduced.
